B_k = {M_j < h for all j <= k}, B_{−1} = Ω, A_k = B_{k−1} \ B_k; the A_k are disjoint, their union is {max_{k<=n} M_k >= h}, and A_k, B_k are functions of Y_1..Y_k. On A_k, M_k = h + (M_k - h), so W_n >= sum_k (M_k - h) 1_{A_k} + h sum_k 1_{A_k} = sum_k (M_k - h) 1_{A_k} + h 1{max_{k<=n} M_k >= h} (the A_k are disjoint with union {max >= h}). Second claim: O_n = E_0[sum_{k<=n}(M_k - h) 1_{A_k}] is nondecreasing in n (every summand is nonnegative) and positive from n_0 with P(A_{n_0}) > 0 because M > h on A_{n_0} for the monitor; so P(ever crossing) <= (1 - O_{n_0}) alpha < alpha. The page now reads: 'Within its budget a group-sequential design with a fixed number of looks can be cheap, as O'Brien and Fleming's power finding above illustrates. A spending design's guarantee also ends with its budget, though.' This is exactly the round-8 proposed replacement. Re-judged on its own merits. (1) Support: the evidence for 'can be cheap' is the B span on line 439 (O'Brien and Fleming, Abstract). I re-read the abstract (OpenAlex, curl 2026-10-19, no email, /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-quant-phd/cdd15252-4236-59f9-8fa8-e63e41e1dc0d/scratchpad/verify9-L01-L02/dl/oa_10_2307_2530245.json): 'comparing two treatments when response to treatment is both dichotomous ... and immediate ... The maximum number (N) of tests and the number (m1 + m2) of observations collected between successive tests is fixed in advance. The overall size of the procedure is shown to be controlled with virtually the same accuracy as the single sample chi-square test ... The power is also found to be virtually the same.' That is a fixed-number-of-looks design, so a power finding about it supports a statement about 'a group-sequential design with a fixed number of looks', and 'can be cheap' is existential and says 'illustrates', not 'all such designs are'. (2) The second sentence moved to 'a spending design' (Lan and DeMets); its support is not the O'Brien-Fleming finding but the page's own argument two sentences later (nested events as in Proposition 6.1, positive probability by part (b), so a design that has spent all of alpha exceeds alpha once an uncovered look is added), which I re-derived (see L01-math-rem69-extralook). The Lan-DeMets abstract (OpenAlex, same date, dl/oa_10_1093_biomet_70_3_659.json) says the boundary 'is determined by alpha*(t), and by past and current decision times, but does not depend on the future decision times or the total number of decision times': a spending design is flexible about the number and timing of looks inside its budget and has no alpha left beyond it, which is what 'ends with its budget' says. (3) Consistency with the rest of the page, re-read: line 439 ('Pocock ... O'Brien and Fleming fix the maximum number of tests ... Lan and DeMets ... replace it with a function alpha*(t)'), quiz item 14's explanation ('Pocock and O'Brien-Fleming fix the number of looks in advance; Lan and DeMets free their number and timing but still spend a fixed alpha'), key-results row 13 and card S7-c146 all separate fixed-look designs from spending designs the same way. The generalization from a fixed-look design's power to 'a spending design' is gone. We also extend our methods to data with infinite variance, but having pth central moment (1 < p < 2).' The page span ('builds confidence sequences for the mean under the sole assumption of a known upper bound on the variance, and extends them to data with infinite variance whose central moment of some order p > 1 is finite') paraphrases it; for infinite variance a finite pth central moment forces p < 2, so 'p > 1' and '1 < p < 2' coincide. Body of the paper checked as well: Assumptions 1-2 (constant conditional mean, conditional variance bounded by a known sigma^2), Theorem 9 (Catoni-style CS), Assumption 3 and Theorem 14 (p-Catoni-style CS, 1 < p <= 2, known bound v_t on the conditional pth central moment). Identification: Ramdas et al. (arXiv v2) section 5.2 cites 'Wang and Ramdas (2023b). Catoni-style confidence sequences for heavy-tailed mean estimation. Stochastic Processes and Applications' for the test supermartingale the first span reports, so the new key is the primary source of that result. Registry: used_by S7; the curriculum Sources line for S7 now lists it (curriculum.json diff). Freshness: published in 2023, arXiv v6 (Feb 2024) has the same abstract; no later version and no published counter-evidence found (related work by Bhatt et al., arXiv 2208.03185, extends the Catoni-style construction to a bounded pth moment and its abstract does not contradict the claim). Note, not a failure: the paper's p-moment extension also needs a known bound on the conditional pth central moment (Assumption 3), which the abstract and the page's sentence leave implicit, as the abstract does. ROMANO'; /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-quant-phd/cdd15252-4236-59f9-8fa8-e63e41e1dc0d/scratchpad/verify9-L01-L02/dl/lr.txt lines 321-330): 'Theorem 2.3. (i) Let the alpha_i be given in (12). For the stepdown procedure (11) with alpha_i given in (12), one cannot increase even one of the constants alpha_i (for i >= k) without violating the k-FWER.' Constants (12): alpha_i = k alpha/s for i <= k and k alpha/(s + k - i) for i > k, which for k = 1 is alpha/(s - i + 1), Holm's. The page's sentence ('prove the analogue for the k-FWER step-down of Lesson 5, whose constants for k = 1 are Holm's: for every i >= k, no constant alpha_i can be increased without violating control of the k-FWER') says exactly that, and L05 Theorem 7.4 states the same constants (2). Part (i) with k = 1 is the sharpness the page proves itself in P4(a) (s + k - i = m - i + 1 true nulls). The paper is peer reviewed, no later version, no counter-evidence applies to a theorem. Scope: the analogue is for the k-FWER step-down, as stated; the page does not attribute the Holm case (k = 1) to the paper beyond 'the analogue', and proves it itself. rows.evidence: unchanged since 765bcb1 (git diff checked); round-23 evidence: Re-derived. m' = m - i + 1 true nulls, c = min(c_i, 1/m'). Since alpha < 1 and c_i > alpha/m' we have c > alpha/m' (both c_i and 1/m' exceed alpha/m'), so m'c > alpha. Construction: i - 1 false nulls at p-value 0 (a false null's p-value is unconstrained; validity is required only of true nulls), true nulls q_j = (U + (j-1)/m') mod 1 for U uniform on [0,1): each q_j is uniform (rotation of the circle), hence valid (P(q_j <= u) = u). rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html Problem P4 solution, 'A false rejection' (lines 443-445)
rows.evidence: unchanged since 765bcb1 (git diff checked); round-23 evidence: Re-derived. Almost surely every q_j > 0 (q_j = 0 only for one value of U), so the i - 1 zeros are p_(1) = ... = p_(i-1) = 0 and p_(i) = min_j q_j belongs to a true null. Zeros pass steps 1, ..., i - 1 because the constants are positive (the step fails only when p_(k) > c_k). If min_j q_j <= c <= c_i, step i passes, so the first failing index is > i and H_(i), a true null, is rejected. Hence FWER >= P(min q <= c) = m'c = min(m' c_i, 1) > alpha (m' c_i > alpha by hypothesis, 1 > alpha). The page states it as an inequality; the equality FWER = min(m' c_i, 1) also holds (step i is then decisive: it passes iff min q <= c_i, and the arcs of length c_i cover the circle when c_i >= 1/m'), which I confirmed numerically; the lesson does not need it. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html Problem P4 solution, 'Zeros are a convenience' (line 448)
rows.evidence: unchanged since 765bcb1 (git diff checked); round-23 evidence: Re-derived. False-null p-values in (0, delta] with delta <= c_j for all j < i: on {delta < min_j q_j <= c} the i - 1 smallest p-values are the false nulls' (each <= delta <= its constant, so steps 1..i-1 pass) and p_(i) = min q <= c <= c_i passes, so a true null is rejected. For delta <= c, P(delta < min q <= c) = m'(c - delta) because the arcs of length delta (<= c <= 1/m') are also disjoint; it exceeds alpha iff delta < c - alpha/m'. The claim is a lower bound on the FWER, as written ('exceeds alpha once delta < c - alpha/m''). Simulated (400 random cases, random m <= 8, random i, random other constants, random false-null p-values in (0, delta]): the estimated FWER was never below m'(c - delta) - 1e-3 and was above alpha whenever delta < c - alpha/m' - 1e-3 (0 violations). rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html Problem P4 solution, 'What it shows' (line 449)
rows.evidence: unchanged since 765bcb1 (git diff checked); round-23 evidence: Checked sentence by sentence. (1) 'A step-down procedure with fixed constants that controls the FWER at level alpha under every joint distribution of valid p-values must have c_k <= alpha/(m + 1 - k) for every k': the contrapositive of the main result (positive constants, alpha < 1). (2) 'Raising constants only adds rejections, because the first failure moves later, so Holm's procedure rejects everything such a procedure rejects, for every vector of p-values': if c_k <= Holm_k for all k then p_(k) > Holm_k implies p_(k) > c_k, so the first failing index of the c-procedure is no later than Holm's and it rejects a subset. (3) 'A gain beyond Holm's needs the dependence between the tests (Lessons 4 and 5)': true for the class the problem treats (p-value step-down with fixed constants, every configuration of true nulls possible, only marginal validity). Outside that class gains can come from logical relations between the hypotheses (Shaffer 1986) as well as from dependence; the sentence is a pointer, sits after the sentence that fixes the class, and is not a graded claim span. Note, not a failure. (4) The T span after it matches Lehmann and Romano Theorem 2.3(ii) (L02-cite-lehmann2005generalizations). rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html line 88 (new figcaption sentence)
rows.evidence: unchanged since 765bcb1 (git diff checked); round-23 evidence: New sentence: 'testing each hypothesis at α/m holds the family-wise error rate at or below α for every m, and here, with independent nulls, at exactly α only when m = 1.' Derivation: by Boole's inequality (as in the proof of Theorem 2.2), the FWER of m true nulls each tested at α/m is at most m·(α/m) = α for any dependence, so 'at or below α for every m' holds. With independent true nulls, FWER = 1 − (1 − α/m)^m. Bernoulli's inequality (1 − x)^m ≥ 1 − mx holds with strict inequality for m ≥ 2 and 0 < x < 1, so FWER < α for m ≥ 2; at m = 1 the FWER is exactly α. Numerical check (scratch scripts/card_numbers.py, python -I, .venv): for α = 0.01..0.10 and m = 1..200, 500, 1000, 5000: 0 violations of FWER ≤ α; strictly below α for every m ≥ 2; |FWER − α| ≤ 1e-15 at m = 1. Values: α = 0.05: FWER(2) = 0.049375, FWER(1000) = 0.048772; α = 0.01: FWER(1000) = 0.009950. The figure's readout and desc in every state agree (row L02-fig-fwer-growth). rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html Problem P2 solution, line 421, the shifted construction
rows.evidence: unchanged since 765bcb1 (git diff checked); round-23 evidence: Re-derived at 535fd80 with s = alpha/2 and p2 = (U + s) mod 1. For U in [0, 1 - s): p2 = U + s > s, so p2 <= s only at U = 0 (p2 = s). For U in [1 - s, 1): p2 = U + s - 1 in [0, s), so p2 <= s. Hence {p2 <= s} = {0} u [1 - s, 1) (exact on the 160000-point rational grid: p2_recheck_535fd80.out section 2, 'A2 equals {0} u [1 - alpha/2, 1) on the grid: True'). Since s < 1 - s for alpha < 1, {U <= s} n {p2 <= s} = {0}, a null set. P(A1) = P(A2) = s, P(A1 n A2) = 0, so P(union) = 2s = alpha. The text 'which meets {U <= alpha/2} only at the null point U = 0, so the two events are disjoint up to a null set and the FWER is again exactly alpha' is TRUE. Monte Carlo: section 3 (mean over 20 seeds of 1,000,000 draws: 0.050002 +- 0.000035). Round-15 FAIL (L02-math-P2-shift-disjoint PASS in round 15) re-checked and still PASS. [a2a631a: L02.html is byte-identical to 765bcb1]

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html Problem P2 solution, line 421 ('E[U((U+s) mod 1)] = 1/3 - s(1-s)/2 ... correlation 1 - 6s(1-s)')
rows.evidence: unchanged since 765bcb1 (git diff checked); round-23 evidence: Derivation at 535fd80. V = (U + s) mod 1 equals U + s on [0, 1-s) and U + s - 1 on [1-s, 1]. E[UV] = int_0^{1-s} u(u+s) du + int_{1-s}^1 u(u+s-1) du = [(1-s)^3/3 + s(1-s)^2/2] + [1/3 - (1-s)/2 + (1-s)^3/6] = (1-s)^2/2 + 1/3 - (1-s)/2 = 1/3 - s(1-s)/2 (using (1-s)^3/2 + s(1-s)^2/2 = (1-s)^2/2 and (1-s)^2/2 - (1-s)/2 = -s(1-s)/2). With E U = E V = 1/2 and Var U = Var V = 1/12 (V uniform), Cov = 1/12 - s(1-s)/2 and corr = 12 Cov = 1 - 6s(1-s). Numerical check: p2_recheck_535fd80.out section 1 evaluates both identities with Fraction arithmetic at 28 rational shifts (k/13, k/97, 1/2, 1/40, 1/20, 1/10, 3/7, 1/4, 2/9, 7/11): both hold exactly at every point (printed: 'points tested: 28'). E[UV] and corr are polynomials of degree at most 3 in s, so 28 exact agreements cover the family. PASS. [a2a631a: L02.html is byte-identical to 765bcb1]

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html line 129 (the paragraph after Example 2.4), first sentence: 'The bound in (1) is attained when the true-null p-values are uniform and their rejection events {p_i <= alpha/m} are pairwise disjoint up to a null set (Problem P2)'
rows.evidence: unchanged since 765bcb1 (git diff checked); round-23 evidence: Re-checked at 45fff85 (line 129 changed: 'disjoint' became 'disjoint up to a null set'). Proof: P(union A_i) = sum_i P(A_i minus union_{j<i} A_j), and P(A_i minus ...) = P(A_i) iff P(A_i and A_j) = 0 for every j < i; so Boole's inequality is an equality iff the pairwise intersections are null (the 'up to a null set' qualifier is exactly right). With uniform true-null p-values, P(p_i <= alpha/m) = alpha/m, so FWER = m0 alpha/m. Construction (P2, exact check p2_p4_exact.out): p1 = U, p2 = (U + alpha/2) mod 1 gives P(A) = P(B) = alpha/2, P(A and B) = 0 and P(A or B) = alpha exactly (alpha = 1/20). Sufficiency is shown; the sentence's 'attained when' is a sufficient condition, which is what it claims. [a2a631a: L02.html is byte-identical to 765bcb1]

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L01.html line 436 (Koning span); arXiv:2501.03982v5 Section 2.2 eqs (3)-(5) and Appendix B.1
rows.evidence: Proof re-derived by me (steps), then spot-checked numerically. Setting: F_n filtration, phi an F-measurable test with values in [0,1], H = {P}, phi_n := E_P[phi | F_n] (eq. 5). (i) Martingale: E_P[phi_n | F_{n-1}] = E_P[E_P[phi | F_n] | F_{n-1}] = E_P[phi | F_{n-1}] = phi_{n-1} by the tower property, since F_{n-1} is contained in F_n. (ii) Values in [0,1] make (phi_n) uniformly integrable; Doob's optional stopping for uniformly integrable martingales gives E_P[phi_tau] = E_P[phi_0] = E_P[phi] for every stopping time tau (paper eq. 9). If phi is valid (E_P[phi] <= alpha), then sup_tau E_P[phi_tau] <= alpha: claim 1. If phi is not valid, every E_P[phi_tau] exceeds alpha: claim 2. (iii) If phi is F_N-measurable for a data-independent N, then phi_N = E_P[phi | F_N] = phi: claim 3. So the span's 'valid ... can be turned into an anytime valid sequential test that matches it after N observations' follows from claims 1 and 3. Numerical spot check: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-quant-phd/cdd15252-4236-59f9-8fa8-e63e41e1dc0d/scratchpad/verify54h-L01-L02/r24/scripts/koning_spot.py (numpy 400,000 paths, N = 20, seed 20261021, scipy.stats.norm), output in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-quant-phd/cdd15252-4236-59f9-8fa8-e63e41e1dc0d/scratchpad/verify54h-L01-L02/r24/logs/koning_spot.txt: valid one-sided z-test phi = 1{S_N > 1.6449 sqrt(N)} with E_P[phi] = 0.05; phi_n = 1 - Phi((c sqrt N - S_n)/sqrt(N - n)) for n < N and phi_N = phi: max |phi_N - phi| = 0.0 (claim 3); phi_0 = 0.05; E_P[phi_n] between 0.0496 and 0.0500 for every n; E_P[phi_tau] = 0.05012, 0.05014, 0.05006, 0.05004 for four stopping times tau <= N (MC s.e. 0.00028, 0.00026, 0.00031, 0.00012). The size-0.10 test gives 0.09943 to 0.10006 for the same stopping times (the claim 2 direction). The displayed 'matches after N' and 'anytime valid' readings hold. PASS.

rows.evidence: unchanged since a2a631a (git diff checked); round-24 evidence: Re-derived: d/dx phi_sigma(x - theta) = ((theta - x)/sigma^2) phi_sigma(x - theta). rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L04.html Proposition 1.3 and proof (lines 77-84); paragraph after it (line 86)
rows.evidence: unchanged since a2a631a (git diff checked); round-24 evidence: Re-derived: by stationarity T Var(dbar) = T^-1 sum_{s,t} gamma(t - s) = sum_{|h| < T} (1 - |h|/T) gamma(h). The terms converge pointwise to gamma(h) and are dominated by |gamma(h)|, which is summable by (i), so T Var(dbar) -> sigma^2_LR. Under H0, DM = (sqrt T dbar/sigma_LR)(sigma_LR/sigma-hat_LR): the first factor -> N(0,1) by (ii); the second -> 1 in probability by (iii) and continuity of x -> sqrt(sigma^2_LR/x) at sigma^2_LR > 0; Slutsky gives the limit, so both the one-sided and two-sided tests have asymptotic level alpha. If mu > 0: DM = sqrt T mu/sigma-hat + sqrt T (dbar - mu)/sigma-hat, where the second term is O_p(1) and the first diverges. Assumptions complete and proof complete. Line 86: (iii) needs l to grow with T, and more slowly than T. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L04.html Remark 1.6 (lines 98-101); card S7-c134
rows.evidence: unchanged since a2a631a (git diff checked); round-24 evidence: Re-checked from scratch (L04 line 100). Combination error e0 - lambda(e0 - e1); MSE = E[e0^2] - 2 lambda E[e0(e0 - e1)] + lambda^2 E[(e0 - e1)^2] (quadratic A - 2 lambda B + lambda^2 C, minimised at B/C with minimum A - B^2/C, checked numerically); lambda* = E[e0(e0 - e1)]/E[(e0 - e1)^2]; encompassing iff E[e0(e0 - e1)] = 0. The repaired example reads 'If both forecasts are unbiased, with mean squared error s^2 and error correlation rho < 1': unbiased means E e = 0, so E[e0 e1] = rho s^2, E[e0(e0 - e1)] = s^2(1 - rho) > 0, E[(e0 - e1)^2] = 2 s^2(1 - rho), lambda* = 1/2, MSE of the equal-weight combination = (2 s^2 + 2 rho s^2)/4 = s^2(1 + rho)/2 < s^2. Simulation (2,000,000 draws, s^2 = 1.69, rho = 0.3, verify8 inline numpy check): lambda* = 0.4995, E[e0(e0 - e1)] = 1.1832 against s^2(1 - rho) = 1.1830, combination MSE 1.0966 against 1.0985. (1) Given the data, the reference law of T^(-1/2) sum_t eps_t d_t has variance T^(-1) sum_t d_t^2 (eps_t = +-1 i.i.d., mean 0, variance 1), so (H1) gives gamma(0). (2) The reference law is symmetric about 0, so its 95% quantile of |.| equals its 97.5% quantile of the signed sum; under (H2) both tend to the 0.975 quantile of N(0, gamma(0)). (3) Quantile identity checked numerically (remark35_limits.out section 1, g = 2.5): 95% quantile of |N(0,g)| = sqrt(g) z_0.975 = 3.0989751615, 97.5% quantile of N(0,g) = 3.0989751615 (equal); z_0.975 = 1.9599639845 (so 1.96 is the 97.5% quantile of N(0,1)). The literal misreading (97.5% quantile of |N(0,1)| = 2.2414027276) is not what the sentence now says. (4) (H3) gives T^(-1/2) sum d_t -> N(0, sigma2_LR); sigma2_LR/gamma(0) = (1+phi)/(1-phi) = 3 at phi = 0.5 and 1.857142857 at phi = 0.3 (remark35_limits.out section 2: direct sums over |h| <= 4000 agree with the closed form). (5) The limit: 2(1 - Phi(1.96 sqrt(gamma0/sigma2))) = 0.2577998945 at phi = 0.5 (page form 2(1 - Phi(1.132)) = 0.2576344344, rounds to 0.258) and 0.1503640418 at phi = 0.3 (page form 2(1 - Phi(1.438)) = 0.1504340541, rounds to 0.150) (remark35_limits.out section 3). rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L03.html Lemma 2.3 (line 102) and its proof; card S7-c217
rows.evidence: unchanged since a2a631a (git diff checked); round-24 evidence: Re-derived. (a) p_(k) <= kq/m iff at least k p-values are <= kq/m: if p_(k) <= kq/m then p_(1..k) are all <= kq/m, so N(k) >= k; if N(k) >= k then the k-th smallest is <= kq/m. Hence R = max{k : N(k) >= k}. (b) If R >= 1, a rejected H_i has p_i <= p_(R) <= Rq/m. Conversely, if p_i <= Rq/m but p_i = p_(j) with j > R, then p_(j) <= Rq/m <= jq/m, so N(j) >= j, contradicting the maximality of R; the zero case is handled (N(1) >= 1 forces R >= 1). (c) Raising a p-value can only lower each N(k), so the largest k with N(k) >= k cannot increase. Numerical spot check (scratch py/spotchecks_r12.py): for 2,000 random p-vectors (m = 10, q = 0.05, mixed scales) the BH rejection set equals {i : p_i <= R q/m} with R = max{k : N(k) >= k} (0 violations), and R does not increase when one randomly chosen p-value is raised (0 violations). Ties: the proof uses the k-th smallest p-value, so ties do not change the count.

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L03.html Proposition 5.3 (line 281) and its proof; card S7-c218
rows.evidence: unchanged since a2a631a (git diff checked); round-24 evidence: Re-derived for rho in [0,1). Given z_i = t, the joint Gaussian (W, z_i) gives W | z_i = t ~ N(sqrt(rho)(t - mu_i), 1 - rho), stochastically increasing in t for rho >= 0 (the constant case rho = 0 is trivially monotone). The other coordinates are z_j = sqrt(rho) W + sqrt(1-rho) eps_j + mu_j with eps_j independent of (W, z_i), so P(z in D' | z_i = t) = E[g(W) | z_i = t], g non-increasing for a decreasing D' (translating all z_j by a common amount). Hence t -> P(z in D' | z_i = t) is non-increasing, which is PRDS (Definition 5.1) on every subset. Numerical spot check (scratch py/spotchecks_r12.py, Monte Carlo 600,000 draws, rho = 0.5, m = 3, D = {p_2 >= 1/2, p_3 >= 1/2}, an increasing set in p-space): P(D | z_1 near t) falls from 0.556 at t = -1 to 0.033 at t = 2 (non-increasing in t), and P(D | p_1 near u) rises from 0.054 at u = 0.05 to 0.708 at u = 0.95 (non-decreasing in u): the PRDS inequality holds in the numerical check. (An earlier attempt used the z-increasing set {z_2 > 0, z_3 > 0}; that set is not an increasing set of p-values, so it was discarded.)

rows.check: 2.3-grade and 2.4-math (Roquain span, grade T with locator 'Theorem 2.5 (arXiv v3, 2020)')
rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L03.html line 409: Roquain and Verzelen show that an estimated null cannot always stand in for the true one: when the nulls are Gaussian with unknown mean and variance, a procedure that asymptotically matches Benjamini-Hochberg run with the true null exists if and only if the number of false nulls is of order less than N/log N, where N is the number of tests
rows.evidence: unchanged since a2a631a (git diff checked); round-24 evidence: Grade: T is the right grade for a result the paper proves with a precisely named theorem (BLUEPRINT section 3: 'proved on the page, or with a precisely cited proof'); the cited proofs are in the arXiv v3 PDF (dl/roquain_arxiv_v3/roquain_v3.txt). Theorem 2.5 (arXiv v3, p. 12 of the paper; image crop dl/roquain_arxiv_v3/thm25-11.png, 200 dpi, read): '(i) for a sparsity k_n >> n/log(n), there exists no (sequence of) AMO procedure that is AMO; (ii) for a sparsity k_n << n/log(n), the sequence of plug-in BH procedure (BH_alpha(theta~, sigma~)) is AMO, for the scaling (theta~, sigma~) given by standard robust estimators (13).' Section 2.7.2 restates it as dense (k_n >> n/log n) and sparse (k_n << n/log n) regimes. Attribution: 'Gaussian with an unknown rescaling parameters (mean and variance) and the alternative distribution is let arbitrary' (abstract) matches 'Gaussian nulls with unknown mean and variance'; the alternative is unrestricted in the paper, which the span does not say (scope is narrower than the paper, not wider; non-blocking). AMO (Definition 2.2) is 'asymptotically mimicking the oracle BH procedure': the span's 'asymptotically matches Benjamini-Hochberg run with the true null' is right. The 'if and only if ... of order less than N/log N' is the abstract's main-result sentence; at the level of orders it is proved: Theorem 3.1 (non-asymptotic lower bound: no procedure with FDR <= c3 is AMO when k2 >= c2 n log(2/alpha)(1+log(k2/k1))/log n) and Theorem 3.2 (plug-in BH is AMO when eta = c2 log(n/alpha)(k/n) v n^(-1/6) <= 0.05, i.e. k of order n/log n or below), so the boundary is order n/log n with constants. Theorem 2.5 itself is stated with >> and <<, so the locator should read 'Theorem 2.5; Theorems 3.1-3.2 (order-level constants)'. That is a precision suggestion, not a failure. Symbols: N is registered as local (notation/notation.json 'about': N is defined in each lesson), and the span defines it in the same sentence. Published-version numbering not verified (R22-cite-roquain2022false).

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L06.html Proposition 4.3 and its proof (lines 269-277): c = sqrt(pi/2)/e = 0.46107; z* with p = 1/e; u(z) = -ln p - c(z + 1/z) >= 0 for 0 < p <= 1/e
rows.evidence: unchanged since 7a0d063 (git diff checked); round-31 evidence: Re-derived. Mills-ratio bounds (Lemma 2.2): x phi(x)/(1 + x^2) <= Q(x) <= phi(x)/x give phi(z) <= Q(z)(z + 1/z) and phi(z)/Q(z) >= z, so e^(-z^2/2) = sqrt(2 pi) phi(z) <= sqrt(pi/2) p (z + 1/z) and it suffices that u(z) = -ln p - c(z + 1/z) >= 0 (page's steps; -ln p = -ln 2 - ln Q, Q' = -phi, so u' = phi/Q - c(1 - 1/z^2)). u' >= z - c(1 - 1/z^2) > 0 for all z > 0 (for z < 1 the right side is negative; for z >= 1 it is below c < 1 <= z), so u is increasing. At p = 1/e, z* = 0.9004526 and u(z*) = 1 - c(z* + 1/z*) = 0.0727888 > 0 (scipy). The page's displayed arithmetic 1 - 0.46107 x 2.01101 = 0.0728 (exact 0.072789 -> 0.0728). For 0 < p <= 1/e, z >= z* so u(z) >= u(z*) > 0. Numerical check on p in (0, 1/e] (200,000 points): min of (-e p ln p - e^(-z^2/2)) = +3.1e-5 > 0; the inequality fails above 1/e (checked on [0.6, 0.99]). PASS.

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L05.html lines 596-598 (equicorrelated normals are MTP2 for 0 <= rho < 1; one-sided p-values; the Simes step at line 598), Lab 5 hypothesis (line 638)
rows.evidence: unchanged since 7a0d063 (git diff checked); round-31 evidence: Re-derived at d10fb51. (a) Sigma = (1-rho) I + rho 11' with Sherman-Morrison: Sigma^{-1} = (1/(1-rho)) [I - rho 11'/(1-rho+m0 rho)], so the off-diagonal entries of Q are -rho/((1-rho)(1-rho+m0 rho)) <= 0 for 0 <= rho < 1. (b) For a normal density with precision Q, log f(z) = const - (1/2) z'Qz; with u = x v y and v = x ^ y, u_i^2 + v_i^2 = x_i^2 + y_i^2, so the diagonal terms cancel and log f(u) + log f(v) - log f(x) - log f(y) = (1/2) sum_{i != j} Q_ij (x_i x_j + y_i y_j - u_i u_j - v_i v_j). The bracket is 0 when (x_i - y_i)(x_j - y_j) >= 0 and equals (x_i - y_i)(x_j - y_j) <= 0 otherwise (checked in the four sign cases), so each term Q_ij times the bracket is >= 0 and f(u) f(v) >= f(x) f(y). Numerical spot check (num/simes_mtp2_check.out): 200,000 random pairs for each of (m, rho) = (3, 0.2), (5, 0.7), (10, 0.95), (20, 0): min(lhs - rhs) = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, -1.4e-14 (rounding), violations 0. (c) One-sided p-values are decreasing in z coordinatewise, which swaps join and meet, and the Jacobian is a product of one-coordinate factors that cancels because {u_i, v_i} = {x_i, y_i}: the true-null p-values are MTP2 as the page says. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L05.html Proposition 7.8 and proof (lines 600-607)
rows.evidence: unchanged since 7a0d063 (git diff checked); round-31 evidence: Re-derived after the rename A -> D. If the original procedure makes no false rejection, the augmented procedure rejects R = R0 + D' with D' = min(D, m - R0) <= D, at most D' of them false; R = 0 gives FDP = 0; otherwise FDP <= D'/(R0 + D') <= D/(R0 + D) because x -> x/(R0 + x) is increasing; and D <= gamma R0/(1 - gamma) iff D (1 - gamma) <= gamma R0 iff D <= gamma (R0 + D), so FDP <= gamma. Hence {FDP > gamma} needs a false rejection by the original procedure: probability <= alpha. Correct, and the letters D, D' no longer clash with the active set A.

Its bound FDR <= m0' q / m' with m' = m0' = m0 gives FDR <= q = alpha for BH at level alpha on the family. (3) When every hypothesis in the family is true, V = R, so FDR = E[1{R >= 1}] = P(R >= 1). (4) BH at level alpha on m0 p-values (step-up) rejects at least one hypothesis iff q_(l) <= l alpha/m0 for some l <= m0. Hence P(union_{l<=m0} {q_(l) <= l alpha/m0}) <= alpha: the Simes inequality for the true-null p-values. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L06.html line 330 ('Exchangeability is assumed, not justified. Bonferroni, Holm and BHY treat every hypothesis alike.') and the Section 6 normal-approximation paragraph
rows.evidence: unchanged since 7a0d063 (git diff checked); round-31 evidence: Classified at 3203b7e as definitional. 'Bonferroni, Holm and BHY treat every hypothesis alike' follows from Definition 2.1 and the step-down and step-up rules (the procedures use the p-values only through their ranks and the values of the statistics; the threshold of Bonferroni is the same at every step). 'Neither holds exactly for small samples, fat tails or serially correlated predictor returns' is a statement about the asymptotic normal approximation (Lemma 2.2 and Theorem 2.3 are asymptotic in the normal approximation; the MBF formula assumes the normal test statistic). Neither is an empirical or literature claim, so neither needs a span under the page's convention, and neither carries a number. PASS.

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L06.html Theorem 4.2 (lines 256-260, proof at 262-266) and the Problem P-solution at line ~405 (the same bound at π0 = 0.99)
rows.evidence: unchanged since 7a0d063 (git diff checked); round-31 evidence: Re-derived at bda7c27. Assumptions: Z ~ N(θ,1), H0: θ = 0, prior π_A on θ under the alternative (Definition 4.1). Step 1: φ(z−θ) ≤ φ(0) for every θ, so ∫φ(z−θ)π_A(dθ) ≤ φ(0) and B(π_A) = φ(z)/∫φ(z−θ)π_A(dθ) ≥ φ(z)/φ(0) = e^(−z²/2); the point mass at θ = z attains it. Step 2: posterior odds of H0 = PO·B(π_A) ≥ PO·e^(−z²/2); x ↦ x/(1+x) is increasing, so (4) holds. Numerical check (c096_check_r22.out): at z = 3, π0 = 0.99: PO = 99, x = PO·MBF = 1.099790657286, x/(1+x) = 0.523762049074; the threshold PO* = e^4.5 = 90.0171313005 gives π0* = 0.9890130574. Alternative priors (part B): B(π_A) ≥ MBF = 0.011108996538 for all 11 structured priors and all 2000 random discrete priors; the point mass gives B − MBF = 0 to floating point. Scope note checked: Definition 4.1 takes π_A as any prior on θ under the alternative and does not exclude θ = 0; on that reading the point mass δ_z attains the bound for every z, including z = 0 (B = 1 = e^0). If the alternative were meant to exclude θ = 0, attainment would hold for z ≠ 0 only, and the infimum would be approached, not attained, at z = 0; the Bayes figure at t = 0 shows the MBF as 1.00, which is the infimum on either reading. The proof's steps are complete and the assumptions are stated. PASS.

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L05.html Definition 6.6 (lines 491-496) and the paragraph at line 499: 'Since V/max(R,1) <= 1{V >= 1}, any simultaneous band at level 1 - alpha, restricted to any selection, has FCR <= alpha'
rows.evidence: unchanged since 7a0d063 (git diff checked); round-31 evidence: Re-derived: for every outcome, V/max(R,1) <= 1{V >= 1} (if V = 0 both sides are 0; if V >= 1 then R >= V >= 1, so V/R <= 1). rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L05.html Theorem 7.4 (line 543, statement and proof lines 544-551), display (2)
rows.evidence: unchanged since 7a0d063 (git diff checked); round-31 evidence: Re-derived the two facts the proof uses. (a) alpha_i of (2) is nondecreasing in i: for i <= k it equals k alpha/m, and for i > k it equals k alpha/(m + k - i), which grows with i and equals k alpha/m at i = k. (b) For i = m - m_0 + k > k (when m_0 < m), k alpha/(m + k - i) = k alpha/m_0, the identity behind 'q_(k) <= alpha_j <= alpha_{m-m_0+k} = k alpha/m_0'. Numerical check (python, exhaustive over 1 <= k <= m < 60 and alpha in {0.05, 0.1}, all m_0 in [k, m]): nondecreasing and identity both hold (True). The Theorem's conclusion is Theorem 2.2 of Lehmann and Romano (R29-arxiv-lehmann2005generalizations). PASS.

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L06.html key-results table, row 4 (raw line 534; grade T; source 'Proved in §3; Lab 2'): 'Reporting the best of K independent null analyses gives a false-positive rate 1-(1-alpha)^K under independence; under any dependence it lies between alpha and min(1,K alpha) (Proposition 3.2)'

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L07.html Corollary 5.2 (lines 405-413), Example 5.5 (line 439-440)
rows.evidence: unchanged since f4190a4 (git diff checked); round-26 evidence: Derivation (steps written out): for f = mu1/sigma1 - mu2/sigma2 the delta method uses the gradient (1/sigma1, -1/sigma2, -mu1/(2 sigma1^3), mu2/(2 sigma2^3)) with respect to (mean1, mean2, var1, var2). Under iid bivariate normal returns with unit variances and correlation rho, the covariance of the moments is Var(mean_i) = 1, Cov(mean1, mean2) = rho, Var(var_i-hat) = 2, Cov(var1-hat, var2-hat) = 2 rho^2, and zero between means and variances (odd moments vanish). Substituting gives V = 2 - 2 rho + (mu1^2 + mu2^2)/2 - rho^2 mu1 mu2, which is formula (5) with mu_i = SR_i. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L08.html section 5 (line 272): containment, monotone expected maximum, and the null-win statement
rows.evidence: unchanged since f4190a4 (git diff checked); round-26 evidence: Re-derived. Let Q_N be the maximum of N null statistics and X_N the new null. Q_N = max(Q_(N-1), X_N) >= Q_(N-1) pointwise, for any joint law of the statistics. (a) E[Q_N] >= E[Q_(N-1)]: the expected maximum cannot fall as N grows. (b) {Z + delta > Q_N} is a subset of {Z + delta > Q_(N-1)}, so the probability that the genuine configuration wins cannot rise (containment, the T span that was already at 584f614). (c) The complement: P(some null beats the genuine) = 1 - P(genuine wins) cannot fall, so 'the null configurations win at least as often' (T). Bound: Lesson 1 Theorem 2.1 (L01.html line 82) states 'Let Z_1, ..., Z_N each have the standard normal distribution, with any joint distribution, and N >= 2. Then E[max Z_n] <= sqrt(2 ln N)'; its proof (Jensen, e^(lambda E M) <= sum E e^(lambda Z_n) = N e^(lambda^2/2), then lambda = sqrt(2 ln N)) is re-derived and holds with no independence. Numerical spot check (scratch scripts/l08_sec5_monotone.py, seed 777, 60,000 draws, N up to 60; output out_l08_sec5_monotone.txt): E[max] of the first N is non-decreasing in N for an equicorrelated law (rho 0.9), independent normals, a comonotone law and a block-random law; at every N it lies below sqrt(2 ln N) (smallest margins 0.9973, 0.5416, 1.1820 and 0.5990); P(genuine wins) with k nulls, k = 1..39, is non-increasing (0.8778, 0.8185, 0.7111, 0.6612, 0.5417, ... ). rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L08.html section 5, T span (line 272): 'The luck, the expected maximum of the nulls, cannot fall as N grows, because adding a null can only raise the maximum; for standard normal null statistics with any joint law it is at most sqrt(2 ln N) (Lesson 1, Theorem 2.1)'
rows.evidence: unchanged since f4190a4 (git diff checked); round-26 evidence: Re-derived at d10fb51. Monotonicity: with N+1 nulls the maximum is the pointwise maximum over N nulls and one more variable, so it is at least the N-null maximum for every outcome, and its expectation cannot fall. Bound: for any joint law of Z_1..Z_N standard normal, e^{lambda E max Z_n} <= E e^{lambda max Z_n} (Jensen) <= sum_n E e^{lambda Z_n} = N e^{lambda^2/2}, so E max Z_n <= ln N / lambda + lambda/2 for every lambda > 0; lambda = sqrt(2 ln N) gives sqrt(2 ln N). The statement matches Lesson 1, Theorem 2.1 (L01.html line 82), whose scope is 'any joint distribution', and the L08 claim uses no wider scope. The index is the page's N (configurations), and the claim uses the N-1 nulls, with sqrt(2 ln(N-1)) <= sqrt(2 ln N). Concept link to L01 def-expected-maximum-sharpe exists (check_dag PASS). rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L07.html Remark 2.9 (line 204): T span 'If SR = 0 and the variance is finite, sqrt(T) SR-hat = (sqrt(T) mu-hat/sigma)(sigma/sigma-hat) -> N(0,1), by the CLT for mu-hat, the LLN for sigma-hat and Slutsky's lemma'
rows.evidence: unchanged since f4190a4 (git diff checked); round-26 evidence: Derivation re-checked step by step. (i) SR-hat = mu-hat/sigma-hat, so sqrt(T) SR-hat = (sqrt(T) mu-hat/sigma)(sigma/sigma-hat) is an identity. (ii) With iid returns, mean mu = SR sigma = 0 and finite variance sigma^2, the CLT gives sqrt(T) mu-hat/sigma -> N(0,1). (iii) sigma-hat^2 = (1/(T-1)) sum (r - r-bar)^2 -> sigma^2 in probability by the LLN applied to r^2 (finite since E r^2 < infinity) and r-bar -> 0; so sigma/sigma-hat -> 1 in probability (the divisor T or T-1 does not matter). (iv) Slutsky gives the limit N(0,1). Nothing beyond finite variance is used. Numerical spot check (scratch num_checks.py, 20000 replications): Student t with 3 df scaled to unit variance, SR = 0: P(z <= -1.6449) = 0.0513 / 0.0502 / 0.0502 and P(z <= 1.6449) = 0.9505 / 0.9500 / 0.9506 at T = 250 / 1000 / 4000 (N(0,1): 0.05 and 0.95); sd(z) = 1.007 / 1.001 / 0.992. The fourth moment is infinite there, so the check is of the claim's sufficiency. Grade T is right (proved on the page). The iid standing assumption is the section 1 assumption ('keep independence'). rows.evidence: unchanged since f4190a4 (git diff checked); round-26 evidence: Re-graded at 50d202e. The block title is T and the block carries a complete proof on the page (Theorem 5.1 plus Slutsky, then the joint-normal sign argument), so T is right; no cite is owed. Re-derived: the naive statistic has limit N(0, theta/(V1+V2)), so the two-sided rejection limit is 2(1 - Phi(z sqrt((V1+V2)/theta))), which is below alpha iff theta < V1+V2. Under SR1 = SR2 = SR and joint normality (5) gives theta = 2(1-rho) + SR^2(1-rho^2) and V1+V2 = 2 + SR^2, so (V1+V2) - theta = rho(2 + SR^2 rho). Grid check (scratch numeric_checks.py, 25 SR values in [0, sqrt2) x 41 rho values in (-1,1)): the identity and sign(V1+V2-theta) = sign(rho) hold everywhere: True. Monte Carlo (numpy, 20000 replications, T = 1260, SR = 0, two normal series): naive rejection 0.1119 at rho = -0.5 (limit 0.1095), 0.0060 at rho = 0.5 (limit 0.0056), 0.0000 at rho = 0.9; paired 0.0515, 0.0492, 0.0508. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L08.html line 95 (C span, data-cite bailey2016probability, no locator): 'Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado and Zhu introduce CSCV as one way to estimate PBO and find, in their own test cases, that it produces reasonable estimates'
rows.evidence: unchanged since f4190a4 (git diff checked); round-26 evidence: Re-checked from scratch at f14987f. Attribution (VERIFIER 2.1): the publisher abstract of Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado and Zhu, The Journal of Computational Finance 20(4) (first published 19 Sep 2016; DOI 10.21314/JCF.2016.322), read on Risk.net with curl -sSL https://www.risk.net/node/2471206 (HTTP 200, 128,762 bytes; final URL https://www.risk.net/journal-of-computational-finance/2471206/the-probability-of-backtest-overfitting). It reads: 'We propose a general framework to assess the probability of backtest overfitting (PBO) ... we call these implementations combinatorially symmetric cross-validation (CSCV). We show that CSCV produces reasonable estimates of PBO for several useful examples.' The 'Need to know' summary reads: 'Results indicate that CSCV provides reasonable estimates of PBO, with relatively small errors.' The span's claim is what the abstract shows: CSCV is introduced as one way to estimate PBO, and the reasonable estimates are for 'several useful examples' that are the authors' own test cases. Scope is correct. Crossref (curl https://api.crossref.org/works/10.21314/jcf.2016.322) carries no abstract; its title, authors and year match the registry record. Grade: C is correct under BLUEPRINT §3 (single-study evidence from the authors' own examples; the venue is peer-reviewed but nothing replicates the result). Counter-evidence: no named published source contests it (row counter-bailey2016probability). The registry-scoped sentence 'No independent study in the registry has yet evaluated its accuracy' is true: a title scan of references/references.json (557 entries; pattern backtest|overfit|PBO|CSCV|combinatorial|selection bias|data snooping|cross-validation) returns 11 titles, none of which names CSCV. Apart from the source of the claim itself (bailey2016probability, which reports the authors' own examples), none of the 11 evaluates CSCV's estimates (bailey2014deflated, bailey2014pseudo, harvey2015backtesting, romano2005stepwise, white2000reality and others are about selection or snooping, not CSCV). Result: PASS.

rows.evidence: unchanged since f4190a4 (git diff checked); round-26 evidence: Crossref record fetched by DOI (curl, no identifying parameters): scratch/r23/crossref_jiang_aoas1983.json. Title 'Endogeneity and moments in time series momentum’s predictability test'; authors Lei Jiang, Liang Peng, Zhongling Qin, Bingduo Yang; The Annals of Applied Statistics 19(1), 701–719; issued 2025-03-01; publisher Institute of Mathematical Statistics. Registry record (references/references.json, entry added at 3e8fe81) gives the same title, authors, year, container, volume 19, issue 1, pages 701-719 and publisher; verify_refs checks in r23-cmd-verify_refs-unit-S7 and r23-cmd-verify_refs-offline pass. Abstract, verbatim from Crossref (JATS tags removed): 'The predictability test is critical in developing momentum trading strategies. In time-series momentum (TSM) tests via linear predictive regressions, the classical and Newey–West t-tests have size distortions because of endogeneity and a lack of enough finite moments. To tackle these issues, this paper proposes a new test that features a model of the error correlations, weighted least squares estimation, and the random weighted bootstrap method. Simulations confirm its accurate size and good power. Empirically, we revisit the evidence in (J. Financ. Econ. 135 (2020) 774–794) and find that the TSM predictability detected by the new test is much more widespread than that by the Newey–West t-tests.' OpenAlex carries the same abstract (scratch/r23/oa_jiang.json; 704 characters in both, identical text). Attribution, sentence by sentence: the surnames are the authors'; 'revisit that evidence' is 'we revisit the evidence in (J. Financ. Econ. 135 (2020) 774–794)', which is Huang, Li, Wang and Zhou (registry huang2020time: JFE 135(3) 774–794, the same volume and pages); 'a test that corrects the size distortions of the classical and Newey–West t-tests' paraphrases 'the classical and Newey–West t-tests have size distortions ... To tackle these issues, this paper proposes a new test ... Simulations confirm its accurate size'. 'corrects' is a fair one-word gloss of 'tackle' plus the authors' simulated 'accurate size'; the simulation basis is the paper's own, so it sits under the B grade of the span; 'much more widespread than the Newey–West tests detect' is 'much more widespread than that by the Newey–West t-tests'. Locator 'Abstract' is the abstract. Publisher full text: https://projecteuclid.org/... returned an Incapsula challenge page (scratch/r23/euclid_jiang.html), so the full text was not read; an arXiv title search returned no record (scratch/r23/arxiv_search_jiang.xml, totalResults 0; the query was ti:'momentum predictability test', which does not match the apostrophe form in the title, so this negative result is weak), and no working-paper version was located. Scope: the sentence does not name the sample; 'that evidence' ties it to the Huang et al. sample, and it does not generalise to other markets. Freshness: published 2025-03-01; no later version found. The Lab 5 twin draws z = sqrt(rho) w + sqrt(1-rho) e + mu (tests/labs/S7/lab-S7-L05-5.py line 39), with mu = 0 on the 450 nulls, so the null p-values are exactly that model. (4) Theorem 5.2 with family size m0 and q = alpha gives FDR <= m0 alpha/m0 = alpha. (5) With all nulls true, V = R, so FDR = E[R/max(R,1)] = P(R >= 1). (6) BH rejects at least one exactly when some q_(l) <= l alpha/m0 (step-up rule), so P(R >= 1) = P(union over l <= m0 of {q_(l) <= l alpha/m0}), the Simes event. Statist. 35(4): the arXiv copy 0710.2258 is the IMS electronic reprint ('This reprint differs from the original in pagination and typographic detail'). Read in full: Algorithm 2.2 (streamlined step-down) replaces the max over I of size k-1 by the k-th statistic over K = {r(|R_j|-k+2),...,r(s)} ; Theorem 3.3: asymptotic k-FWER control via Algorithm 2.2 (the conclusions of Theorem 3.1 continue to hold); Remark 3.2: first point 'the latter will reject all the hypotheses rejected by the former and potentially some further ones' (rejects at least as much); the proofs of Theorems 3.1 and 3.3 'rely on asymptotic arguments' (they establish control only asymptotically). Algorithm 4.1 (sequential k-FWER with stop rule N_j < k_j/gamma - 1) and Theorem 4.1 (lim sup P(FDP > gamma) <= alpha) match the lesson's exceedance sentence. The lesson's new text is accurate. rows.location: grader/test_project.py::test_every_new_block_can_start_at_any_period (new)
rows.evidence: unchanged since c16bcf1 (git diff checked); round-16 evidence: Judged against the contract: stationary_bootstrap_indices(n_obs, mean_block, rng) 'start at a uniform index; at each later step, with probability 1/mean_block start a new block at a uniform index, otherwise move to (previous + 1) mod n_obs'. With mean_block = 1.0 every later step starts a new block, so every position is a uniform draw on 0..n-1, and each index's share over all positions is 1/n = 0.2. The test runs 2000 resamples of n = 5 (10000 draws), and asserts each share is within 0.02 of 0.2. The standard error of a share is sqrt(0.2 x 0.8 / 10000) = 0.004, so the tolerance is 5 standard errors (false-failure probability about 1e-6 per index). The assertion covers every position (not only the first), which is what the contract says. Reference: passes seeds 0-49. Loop-based variant: passes seeds 0-9. Pyodide: 0.12 s (seed 0) and 0.13 s (seed 190092024). It kills x08 at seed 0. Message: 'A new block starts at a uniformly drawn period at every step ... (contract: stationary_bootstrap_indices).' It names the property and does not reveal the answer.

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/cards.json S7-c172 (L05, grade T, cite lehmann2005generalizations); L05.html Lemma 7.6 and its proof (line 579 changed)
rows.evidence: Card: 'State the union bound for ordered p-values that generalizes Hommel's.' Back: for valid p-values, M <= t, 0 = beta_0 <= ... <= beta_M <= 1, under any dependence P(union_{l<=M}{p_(l) <= beta_l}) <= t sum_{l=1}^{M}(beta_l - beta_{l-1})/l; with beta_l = l alpha/t and M = t this is Hommel's bound alpha c(t) (Lemma 7.6). Lemma 7.6 (L05 section 7) states the same inequality for valid p-values with M <= t and 0 = beta_0 <= ... <= beta_M <= 1, for any joint distribution: the card matches the statement. Grade T is right because the lemma is proved on the page. I re-derived the proof: (i) J = smallest l <= M with p_(l) <= beta_l, theta_l = P(J = l); J 1{J<=j} <= S_j uses beta nondecreasing; E[S_j] <= t beta_j uses validity; (ii) weights w_j = 1/(j(j+1)) for j < M and w_M = 1/M telescope: sum_{j=l}^{M} w_j = 1/l (checked for M <= 14); (iii) summation by parts sum_{l=1}^{M}(beta_l - beta_{l-1})/l = sum_{j<M} beta_j/(j(j+1)) + beta_M/M (max error 2.2e-16 over 2000 random beta, r17-cmd-lemma76-check); (iv) Monte Carlo under positively dependent valid p-values (Gaussian copula, n = 200,000, five cases) gives P(union) below the bound in every case. The sentence changed at line 579 ('which the lemma generalizes to any M <= t and any nondecreasing beta') is what the proof shows. PASS.

rows.location: ledgers/S7/mutants/y29_pbo_ranks_configurations_from_the_top.py (new this round)
rows.evidence: New mutant, a full solution module: one changed line ('rank = 1.0 + lower + 0.5 * ties' replaced by 'rank = 1.0 + (n_strategies - 1 - lower - ties) + 0.5 * ties'). Ranking from the top gives rank' = N + 1 - rank, so omega' = 1 - omega and every logit changes sign: the PBO becomes the share of logits at or above zero. Plausible student error: reversed rank direction. KILLED y29_pbo_ranks_configurations_from_the_top.py: probability_of_backtest_overfitting ranks each out-of-sample configuration from the top (rank 1 for the best), which reverses every logit's sign, so the PBO becomes the share of logits at or above zero. -> test_pbo_matches_cscv_definition (seed 0).

Sharpe-ratio standard error divides the variance bracket by n instead of n - 1.
Sharpe-ratio standard error uses (kurtosis - 3)/4 in the bracket, mixing the excess-kurtosis form with raw kurtosis.
Deflated Sharpe ratio takes the population variance (ddof=0) of the trial Sharpe ratios instead of ddof=1.
expected_max_sharpe at N = 1 returns 0.0 instead of sr_mean (forgets the shift when there is no selection).
Stationary bootstrap never wraps around: a block that would run past the last period starts a new block instead of continuing at index 0.
Stationary bootstrap uses mean_block as the restart probability (1/p in place of p), so every step starts a new block.

Romano-Wolf is not studentized: it compares raw mean differentials with centred bootstrap means instead of t-statistics.

Step-down critical value uses the floor((1-alpha)B)-th order statistic instead of the ceil((1-alpha)B)-th.
Step-down never recomputes the critical value: one max-T critical value over all hypotheses (single-step test).

romano_wolf guards the overflow of the re-expressed column mean but not of the studentized difference, so a resample far smaller than its column warns (overflow in divide) instead of giving the contract's quiet +-inf statistic.

integrity_report computes the trials' t-statistics for the BH p-values on the unscaled returns, so a trial set of tiny or huge returns (2**-600 or 2**600 times ordinary ones) underflows or overflows its variances and warns.
integrity_report does not forward its seed, so its Romano-Wolf bootstrap is always drawn from np.random.default_rng(0) whatever seed the caller passes.
integrity_report does not forward alpha, so its Romano-Wolf rejections always use romano_wolf's default level 0.05 whatever alpha the caller passes.
deflated_sharpe_ratio applies the zero-variance rule of a return series to trial_sharpes, so equal trial Sharpe ratios (variance 0, so SR0 = 0) raise ValueError instead of giving the PSR against 0.
integrity_report validates q but runs Benjamini-Hochberg at alpha, the StepM level, so bh_rejections ignore the caller's q.
integrity_report does not forward mean_block, so its Romano-Wolf bootstrap always uses romano_wolf's default mean block length 10 whatever the caller passes.
integrity_report computes the trials' t-statistics for the BH p-values with np.std's default ddof=0 instead of std(ddof=1).

Step-down uses each hypothesis's own bootstrap quantile (the ceil((1-alpha)B)-th smallest t*_bk of column k) instead of the quantile of the maximum over the active set, so it controls no family-wise error.
CSCV forms its S blocks by interleaving rows (block i holds rows i, i+S, i+2S, ...) instead of consecutive runs of periods.
integrity_report annualizes the selected Sharpe ratio by multiplying by periods_per_year instead of its square root.
Stationary bootstrap draws block starts with rng.integers(0, n - 1), an exclusive upper bound one too low, so the last period never starts a block.
expected_max_sharpe hard-codes Lesson 7 Example 3.2's bracket 2.1895 for N = 40 trials instead of evaluating the formula at the given N.
deflated_sharpe_ratio ignores an explicit n_trials and always deflates by len(trial_sharpes).
probabilistic_sharpe_ratio subtracts in the wrong order, Phi((SR* - SR)/se), so it returns one minus the PSR.
integrity_report ignores TrialSet.selected and reports on the trial with the highest Sharpe ratio, which is only the proposed strategy when the proposal is the in-sample best.
stepdown_rejections removes each rejected hypothesis from the maximum by writing -inf into its column of the caller's t_boot, so the caller's bootstrap matrix is mutated.
CSCV breaks an in-sample tie for the best configuration in favour of the highest index instead of the lowest.
integrity_report prints a one-line summary of its result, a leftover debugging statement the contract forbids.
romano_wolf multiplies the caller's differentials matrix by its per-column power of two in place, so the caller's data change although every decision stays the same.
benjamini_hochberg sorts the caller's p-value array in place after taking its ordering, so the caller's array is mutated although the returned mask is right.
integrity_report annualizes the selected Sharpe ratio with a hard-coded sqrt(252), ignoring the trial set's periods_per_year.
TrialSet.from_backtest takes the in-sample best column as selected instead of the backtest result's own selected attribute.
benjamini_hochberg, stepdown_rejections and romano_wolf accept a level of exactly 1 (0 < level <= 1), although the contract requires 0 < q < 1 and 0 < alpha < 1.
integrity_report requires T > 4 instead of T >= 4, so the smallest trial set the contract allows (four periods, two-period CSCV halves) raises ValueError.
stationary_bootstrap_indices rejects mean_block == 1 (requires > 1), although the contract allows any mean_block >= 1, which is the iid bootstrap.
integrity_report takes each trial's p-value as 1 - PSR(trial, 0), the skewness-and-kurtosis-adjusted tail, instead of the contract's 1 - Phi(mean / (std / sqrt(T))).
The step-down loop compares absolute statistics, |t| against the maximum of |t*|, as for a two-sided test, although each hypothesis is one-sided (E[d] <= 0).
probability_of_backtest_overfitting evaluates only the first 500 splits in itertools order to save time, so a PBO with 12 or more blocks (924 or more splits) is not the share over all of them.
CSCV ranks configurations by their mean return instead of their Sharpe ratio, in sample and out of sample.
integrity_report returns the Benjamini-Hochberg mask in order of increasing p-value instead of the trials' column order.
benjamini_hochberg returns a stored mask when it recognises the seed-0 instance's p-values and otherwise uses the step-down rule (stop at the first p-value above its line).
integrity_report builds each trial's t-statistic for the p-values with sqrt(T - 1) in the standard error instead of sqrt(T).
stationary_bootstrap_indices truncates mean_block to an integer with int(), so a mean block of 2.5 behaves as 2.
Series validation requires at least 3 observations instead of 2, so a series of exactly two observations raises ValueError.
romano_wolf requires n_boot >= 2 instead of n_boot >= 1, so a single bootstrap draw raises ValueError.
stepdown_rejections requires B >= 2 bootstrap draws instead of B >= 1.
stationary_bootstrap_indices requires n_obs >= 2 instead of n_obs >= 1.
deflated_sharpe_ratio requires at least 3 trial Sharpe ratios instead of 2.
deflated_sharpe_ratio requires an explicit n_trials of at least 2, so n_trials = 1 (a valid single-trial deflation, SR0 = 0) raises ValueError.
sharpe_ratio_std requires n_obs >= 3 instead of n_obs >= 2, so the smallest sample the contract allows raises ValueError.
PBOResult, TrialSet and IntegrityReport are plain dataclasses, not frozen=True as the contract says, so their fields can be reassigned.
benjamini_hochberg, stepdown_rejections and romano_wolf return a Python list of bools instead of the NDArray[np.bool_] the contract names.
benjamini_hochberg requires 0 < p < 1, so a p-value of exactly 0 or exactly 1 raises ValueError although the contract allows [0, 1].
romano_wolf does not centre the bootstrap statistics at the observed mean: t*_bk = mean(d*_k) / (std(d*_k, ddof=1) / sqrt(T)).
romano_wolf runs the step-down at alpha / 2 (a two-sided level) although each hypothesis is one-sided.
integrity_report does not forward n_boot, so its Romano-Wolf bootstrap always uses 1000 draws.
TrialSet bounds selected by 0 <= selected < N - 1 (an off-by-one), so the last column cannot be the proposed strategy.
integrity_report defaults to n_blocks = 8 instead of the contract's 16.
integrity_report defaults to n_boot = 500 instead of the contract's 1000.
romano_wolf defaults to mean_block = 5.0 instead of the contract's 10.0.
probability_of_backtest_overfitting defaults to n_blocks = 8 instead of the contract's 16.
integrity_report defaults to seed = 1 instead of the contract's 0.
romano_wolf defaults to alpha = 0.10 instead of the contract's 0.05.

stationary_bootstrap_indices cuts the resample into fixed blocks of round(mean_block) periods (a moving-block bootstrap), instead of geometric block lengths that restart with probability 1/mean_block.
benjamini_hochberg leaves the p-values equal to 1 out of the number of hypotheses m, as if they were not tests, so the step-up lines use the smaller count.
benjamini_hochberg counts each distinct p-value once in m (np.unique), so ties among rounded p-values shrink the number of hypotheses in the step-up lines.
romano_wolf returns its decision vector in reverse column order, an indexing error that leaves each decision with the wrong strategy when there are several columns.
romano_wolf squeezes its decision vector with np.squeeze, so a single differentials column returns a 0-d array rather than one boolean per column.
stepdown_rejections takes its critical value as np.quantile(maxima, 1 - alpha, method='higher') instead of the ceil((1-alpha)B)-th order statistic.
sample_kurtosis divides the fourth central moment by the squared sample variance with ddof=1 (m4 over s**4), mixing the sample and the moment estimators.
stationary_bootstrap_indices draws every block start after the first from periods 1..n-1, so period 0 is never the start of a new block (an off-by-one in the integers bound).
expected_max_sharpe swaps the Euler-Mascheroni weights: gamma multiplies the 1/N quantile and 1 - gamma the 1/(N e) quantile.
stationary_bootstrap_indices starts a new block with probability 1/(mean_block + 1), an off-by-one in the block-length parameter.
CSCV's out-of-sample rank counts the chosen configuration as one of its own ties, so every rank is 0.5 too high.
Romano-Wolf step-down takes its critical value from the maxima over all hypotheses, not over the ones still active.
Step-down critical value is the (floor((1-alpha) B) + 1)-th order statistic, one rank above the contract's ceil((1-alpha) B)-th when (1-alpha) B is an integer.
Stationary bootstrap wraps the time index modulo n_obs - 1, so the last period is never drawn after the first block start.
Romano-Wolf's bootstrap statistics divide by sqrt(T - 1), the T - 1 convention of the Sharpe-ratio standard error carried into the t* draws, while the observed statistics keep sqrt(T).
probabilistic_sharpe_ratio computes its standard error with T - 1 periods instead of T, an off-by-one in the sample size.
sharpe_ratio_std adds the skewness term (+skew*SR) to the variance bracket instead of subtracting it, a sign error in the non-normal standard error.
Romano-Wolf's constant-resample branch takes the means from the unscaled differentials but the standard error from the rescaled ones, so units mix whenever a column is not near unit magnitude.
CSCV's out-of-sample rank takes the largest rank of a tie (1 + #lower + #others equal) instead of the average rank, so tied configurations are ranked too high.
Benjamini-Hochberg compares every ordered p-value with the Bonferroni line q/m instead of the rank line kq/m, so the step-up rejects by the largest p-value under q/m.
CSCV keeps only the splits whose in-sample half contains block 0, half of the C(S, S/2) splits, so the logit distribution is estimated from a subset of the splits.
The expected maximum uses Phi^-1(1 - 1/(N+1)) in place of Phi^-1(1 - 1/N) in its first term, an off-by-one in the number of trials.

sample_skewness returns the bias-corrected adjusted Fisher-Pearson estimator g1 * sqrt(n(n-1))/(n-2) instead of the moment estimator m3 / m2**1.5, so the skewness fed to the PSR and to the Sharpe ratio's standard error is inflated.

CSCV scores the in-sample winner on the same blocks it was chosen from (the out-of-sample set is the in-sample half, the complement forgotten), so the winner always ranks first out of sample and the PBO is zero.

expected_max_sharpe multiplies the z-score by sr_variance, the variance of the Sharpe estimates, instead of its square root, so the expected maximum scales with the variance and the DSR's benchmark SR0 is too small when the variance is below one.
Stationary bootstrap draws block starts from 0..n-2 (rng.integers(0, n - 1)), so the last period never starts a block.
DSR benchmark is the mean of the trial Sharpe ratios (the average trial) instead of their expected maximum under the null.
PSR returns the one-sided p-value 1 - Phi(z) instead of Phi(z), the probability that the true Sharpe ratio exceeds the benchmark.
CSCV relative rank divides by the number of strategies N instead of N + 1, so the logit of the top rank is infinite and the logits differ from the definition.
sharpe_ratio divides the mean by the population standard deviation (ddof=0) instead of the sample one (ddof=1), inflating every Sharpe ratio by sqrt(T/(T-1)).
stationary_bootstrap_indices ignores mean_block and starts a new block at every step, which is the i.i.d. bootstrap rather than the stationary one.
deflated_sharpe_ratio uses the single-trial variance 1/T of a Sharpe ratio estimate as the trial variance in the expected maximum, instead of the variance of the trials' Sharpe ratios.
sharpe_ratio_std uses (kurtosis - 1)/2 instead of (kurtosis - 1)/4 in the variance bracket, doubling the kurtosis term of the non-normal standard error.
benjamini_hochberg compares the k-th smallest p-value with the line (k-1) q / m, a 0-based rank in the step-up line, so every line sits one step low.
probability_of_backtest_overfitting chooses the configuration by its out-of-sample metric (it reads the test half), so the chosen configuration always ranks first out of sample and the PBO is zero.
stationary_bootstrap_indices never starts a new block after the first period, so every resample is one circular block (a restart probability of zero) and its block length is infinite, not mean_block.

probability_of_backtest_overfitting ranks each out-of-sample configuration from the top (rank 1 for the best), which reverses every logit's sign, so the PBO becomes the share of logits at or above zero.
integrity_report gives every trial the selected column's one-sided p-value (a copy-paste slip), so the Benjamini-Hochberg mask is computed from one repeated p-value.
